P1.evidence: Full four-part frame delivered — 'where we're at today, which we already kind of dove in a little bit, specifically where we want to go, what's genuinely missing to get there, and then anything that's been getting in the way as well' — and agreement taken: 'That'll sound good? Yeah.' P1a is partial: the application was referenced in passing ('I saw in your applications, like healthcare startup or something like that?') but nothing was read back at the open. P1d is partial because the prospect volunteered a complete two-minute overview before the frame was set, so the open question was never actually asked; the rep's response was 'thanks for giving me the overview.' Minor sequencing point, not a substantive failure.

P2.evidence: Strong throughout. Age, height and weight asked directly. Work covered including sedentary load and daily step count. P2d is a clear hit with good follow-up — 'any health conditions, injuries, anything like that?' produced the bilateral shoulder dislocations, and the rep asked the right next question, 'How'd you dislocate them?', which surfaced that one of the mechanisms was rolling over in bed. Training week captured from the prospect's actual training log. Diet is the best-run check on the call, with three layers of follow-up: what the diet looks like, where the fat comes in, and 'Why do you fall off when you do fall off?'. Sleep and energy asked and then genuinely probed: 'what's keeping you from being consistent with work and working out and still getting sleep on top of it?'. P2c partial for the usual reason — hereditary conditions never asked. P2f partial: results from current training were not asked directly, only approached through the physique question.

P3.evidence: The best goals work in the batch. P3a asked directly about physique and aesthetics and got a precise answer, 175 lb and roughly 16% on a DEXA. P3b swept for the rest: 'what are some of the other goals that you're having physically right now with your body'. P3d asked cleanly — 'outside of just obvious the physical aspect of this... what's actually driving all of this for you?' — and then the rep pushed twice more rather than accepting the first answer, including 'it takes a special type of person to be doing these things on a regular basis... what's the drive behind this?'. That persistence is what produced the real material: adventure, risk, and the fear of becoming the kind of athlete who trains four hours a day and is absent from his family. P3h is a genuine reflect-back and the only creative one in the batch — 'Michelangelo had his sculptures and Elon Musk has his business. I get the sense that this is kind of like your art' — refined when it did not quite land into 'it's like something very personal to you', which got 'Yeah, I think so. I would agree with that.' P3g reached kids and legacy explicitly. P3c and P3f are partial only because the specific scripted questions were not asked; the prospect volunteered the equivalent material.

P4.evidence: Half of this phase ran well and the half that mattered did not. P4c and P4d were asked properly and produced the structural answer — 'Why do you fall off when you do fall off?' and 'what's keeping you from being consistent... Like what happens where we can't do all of it?' — which the prospect answered with busyness and travel, then narrowed to travel himself. P4e is a hit: he named the gap without prompting, 'I just like pick random workouts from random people. There's no real strategy behind it.' P4f is the miss that decided the call. This prospect's entire objection was that he could do it himself, he said so at minute 32 and repeated it at minute 47, and he was never once asked why he had not already done it or why he could not stick to it alone. The rep diagnosed this himself in his manager 1-1 the same day: 'in the discovery, I didn't ask the DIY stuff... I could have asked him, it's like, well, dude, what have you been trying so far? Like, why not just do this yourself out of curiosity? Like, I could have asked that stuff, and I didn't.' That is the correct diagnosis.

P5.evidence: The only genuine consequence-frame attempt in this batch, and it was well set up: 'what we found is that our clients who really get the best results with this have a super, super strong reason why... a lot of times the why also gets amplified when we look at what happens if we don't actually really get this dialed in... if we don't get this dialed in in the next four to six months or whatever, however long November is, what would life actually look like a couple of years down the road?' The prospect batted it straight back — 'I mean, like I will get it dialed in... I'll get it dialed in one way or another' — and the rep folded immediately: 'Yeah. Okay. Cool. Cool. All right. We won't spend much time on that.' That answer was not a deflection to move past, it was the objection of the entire call arriving twenty-five minutes early and announcing itself. Not asking 'why not?' there is the single highest-leverage miss on this recording. Credit for asking; the whole phase turns on what happens after the first resistance, and this is now the third call in the batch where the rep abandoned P5 on the first push-back.

P6.evidence: P6a asked and answered: 'training, nutrition, accountability, lifelong success, all built around your life specifically. If we had all those things dialed in, do you feel like that would be everything that you need to basically get this all dialed in before the baby comes?' — 'Yeah.' P6b ran through the 1-to-10 instrument and, to the rep's credit, he asked the follow-up that matters: 'other than just never having purchased something from like a Instagram influencer before, there anything else that's keeping it from being less than like a 10 out of 10?'. P6c is a clear miss. The score was a seven or eight, not a yes, and the stated condition was explicitly commercial — 'if it's, the price makes sense, you know, sign up today.' The script says a clear YES before presenting and a return to Phase 5 on hesitation. A seven out of ten from a prospect who has already said he will get there on his own is hesitation, and the rep moved to price anyway.

P11.evidence: Close attempted repeatedly and refused outright — 'I'm not going to swipe a card on this call for that much.' No payment, so steps two to four were unreachable. Nothing concrete was secured as a fallback: no deposit, no held onboarding slot, no booked follow-up call, only 'I'll send you a text in a couple of days.' Note for the record that what was pursued in place of a clean close was a descending price ladder and an unauthorised refund term, which is a P11 failure compounded rather than mitigated.

objection_plays.detail: Trigger unmistakable: '$250 a month was the maximum that I was ready to pull the trigger on right now.' Two moves ran and ran well. The isolate: 'outside of finances though, like, I do want to ask, like, do you feel that everything we covered... will solve all the things that we're looking for?' answered yes. And a sharp diagnostic: 'it's not the fact that we don't have it, it's just it's more a little bit of uncertainty around the value currently. Is that what I'm understanding?' — which correctly identified this as a value question, not an affordability one. Everything after that went the wrong way. The scripted response to a value gap is to build value and, if needed, to explore breaking the payment up; not one of the six financial-picture questions was asked — no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no credit cards, no available credit, no used-versus-available, no investments — and no payment plan was ever offered. Instead the price itself moved twice. The manager's assessment the same day was that this was a value gap and that the right move was to name it honestly and, failing that, to route him to the cheaper product.

Triggered at least four times, from 'we'll have to think about it' through 'Let me think about it. I'm not going to swipe a card on this call.' Several moves ran. The can-this-get-you-there move: 'if we taught you what you needed to know to figure out the nutrition, have that consistency, if you knew how to modify your workouts directly to help out with endurance... would it be worth 3000?' answered 'Uh, yes, totally.' And the what's-actually-coming-up move, asked well: 'what's coming up for us to sort through on that? Like what are we actually weighing on that?' — which produced the genuinely useful answer that he intended to go price-compare on Instagram. The university-versus-scholarship analogy is a competent improvised value reframe. What did not run: 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here — when do you make a different decision?', and the closing 'are you sure? nothing else keeping you from being 100% in?'. Scored partial rather than higher because the moves that ran were interleaved with price cuts, so the play was never allowed to work on its own terms.

The playbook's own documented gap, in its clearest form yet. The prospect's objection was not price and not a competitor — it was that he is capable of doing this himself and the only question is speed: 'if it took me on my own eight months or nine months, would I get to the same point, but just be slower at it? And with less of a financial investment.' He restated it three times and closed with it. There is no scripted play for a self-directed prospect who is correct that he can do it alone, and the rep improvised an authority claim — 'he is kind of the number one person on the planet for kettlebells... there really isn't anybody else' — which the prospect politely sidestepped by clarifying he does not want to become a kettlebell expert, only to look and perform how he wants. The manager supplied the missing play in the debrief the same day, and it should be written into the script verbatim: concede the point first — 'you probably are capable of doing it on your own. You probably don't need Trevor, but that's not the reason why people invest in Trevor' — then reframe to premium and speed, then explicitly permit the cheaper route if that is where the prospect actually is.

notes: Genuinely good discovery and the best reflect-back in the batch, wrapped around a collapse at the close. Three coaching actions, in order of value. First, P5: the prospect handed over the objection at minute 32 — 'I will get it dialed in one way or another' — and the rep said 'we won't spend much time on that' and moved on. That sentence needed 'why not?' and ten more minutes, not a retreat. Second, run P4f whenever the prospect is self-directed and successful; the rep identified this omission himself and it is the same failure as the Tom Eldon call. Third, and most seriously, the response to a value gap here was three descending prices and an invented refund term rather than any of the scripted money play — no financial-picture question was asked at any point on a 68-minute call that ended in a price negotiation.
